sources.note: Melanesia-wide coverage bibliography (one entry per language listing its most extensive descriptive sources with type tags); entry lists only Chowning 1985 Sengseng and its neighbours (PL C-88) [overview, comparative]; no phonology or grammar recorded for this language and no stress or tone content anywhere in the entry.

sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 2001. Language endangerment in the insular Greater Pacific area, and the New Guinea area in particular. In Andrew Pawley, Malcolm Ross & Darrell Tryon (eds), The boy from Bundaberg: studies in Melanesian linguistics in honour of Tom Dutton, 383-398. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics 514.

Chowning, Ann. 1996. Relations among languages of West New Britain: an assessment of recent theories and evidence. In M.D. Ross (ed.), Studies in languages of New Britain and New Ireland 1, 7-62. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-135.
sources.note: Karore discussed only for subgrouping (sec. 8.3.1, p.33: easternmost Pasismanua language; Throops misidentified it; Throop & Ross 1994 include it in the 'Pasismanua dialect chain') and in a handful of lexical comparisons (tot 'she', kenin 'food'). No stress or accent statement anywhere in the paper.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm D. 1996. Introduction. In Ross (ed.), Studies in languages of New Britain and New Ireland 1, 1-6. Pacific Linguistics C-135.
Ross, Malcolm D. 1988. Proto Oceanic and the Austronesian languages of Western Melanesia. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-98.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201.R67 1988)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201 .R67 1988
sources.note: Karore not mentioned at all (a full-text search for stress/accent); the Pasismanua chain figures only in the SW New Britain subgrouping (Figure 5, ch. 6). No stress statement for any Pasismanua language.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1985. Rapid lexical change and aberrant Melanesian languages: Sengseng and its neighbours. In A. Pawley & L. Carrington (eds), Austronesian linguistics at the 15th Pacific Science Congress, 169-198. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-88.
sources.note: Glottolog's most extensive description of Karore (level wordlist-or-less). Karore appears only as a named Pasismanua language (p.170), in a few cognate sets (Karore /r/ = Sengseng /h/, e.g. mirit 'shoulder', vrok, sirit) and in fn.3 (p.192) on its location between the Andru and Johanna rivers. No phonology of Karore and nothing on stress in any language.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1976. Austronesian languages: New Britain. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study 2: Austronesian languages, 365-386. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-39.
sources.note: Karore is item 27 of the Whiteman family list. Only prosodic remark is group-level, p.379: 'There are a few suggestive resemblances, including the possibility of phonemic tone in some Whiteman languages' (about links to north New Guinea languages); no Karore-specific data, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1976. History of research in Austronesian languages: New Britain. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study 2: Austronesian languages, 179-196. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-39.
sources.note: no phonology content (the word 'stressed' occurs only in the sense 'emphasised')

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1969. The Austronesian languages of New Britain. In A. Capell, A. Chowning & S.A. Wurm, Papers in linguistics of Melanesia No. 2, 17-45. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics A-21.
sources.note: Sec. 3.71 names Karore as one of the four Pasismanua 'dialects' (Miu, Kaulong, Sengseng, Karore); Chowning's own Karore wordlist is listed among the survey's sources. No phonological description of Karore; the stress remarks in this volume belong to Wurm's Reef Islands-Santa Cruz section, not New Britain.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Karore language' (stub); Wikidata Q6373260
sources.note: Ethnologue-derived stub: c.550 speakers (2003) between the Andru and Johanna rivers; no phonology, no references beyond Ethnologue/ELP/UNESCO ids.

sources.citation: Throop, Craig & Malcolm D. Ross. 1994. Kaulong. In D.T. Tryon (ed.), Comparative Austronesian dictionary 1, 719-726. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Sketch of the closest well-described Pasismanua language (Kaulong, kaul1240), includes phonology; Chowning 1996 says it groups Karore in the 'Pasismanua dialect chain'. Would give the family-level stress pattern but is not a Karore description.

sources.citation: Throop, Craig & Linda Throop. 1980. The languages and communities of the Kandrian inland region. In R.L. Johnston (ed.), Language, communication and development in New Britain, 225-240 (wordlists pp.257-259). Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics.

sources.note: Only other published work with Pasismanua field data that touches the Karore area; a survey, so a stress statement is unlikely, and Chowning notes it misidentified Karore as Arawe/Palik. Worth checking the wordlist conventions for stress marks.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. Unpublished Karore wordlist / fieldnotes (cited as her own source for Karore in Chowning 1969, 1985, 1996).

sources.note: The only first-hand Karore data known to exist; if archived (e.g., PARADISEC or her papers) it might mark stress. Never published.
